summary: For ages 6-7, this topic builds the habit of looking for and expressing regularity in repeated reasoning (MP8): deriving a near-double from a known double (6+7 = 6+6+1 = 13), noticing that subtracting 10 from a two-digit number drops the tens digit by one, and stating a sequence rule ('+5 each time starting from 5, so the ones digit alternates 5, 0') — then TESTING that rule on a fresh case rather than trusting it from one or two examples. Core teaching moves: place a known fact adjacent to the derived one so the adjustment is seen not recomputed, press for the rule in the child's own words, and always test the generalisation on a new case.
misconceptions: Recomputes 6+7 from one, not seeing it as the known double 6+6 plus 1
Applies the near-double adjustment wrongly (adds 2, or doubles the larger number)
States a rule from one or two cases and assumes it holds without testing
Subtracts 10 by changing the ones digit or counting back in ones instead of dropping the tens digit

activities.title: Near-doubles builder: the double plus one
steps: Set out two rows of 6 cubes (or two ten-frames of 6) and confirm the double: 6+6=12.
Add exactly ONE more cube to one row and say the new total: 6+7=13. State it as 'the double I know, and one more'.
Repeat for 6+8 ('two more than the double, so 14') and for another double you know, e.g. 7+7=14 so 7+8=15.
Say aloud which double you used and how many you adjusted by, before giving the total.
activities.insight: A near-double can be derived from an adjacent known double by adjusting, instead of counting up from one.

activities.title: State a rule, then test it
steps: Lay out the first few terms of a sequence (e.g. 5, 10, 15, 20) and say the repeating step out loud: '+5, +5, +5'. Optionally show the equal +5 jumps on a number line or bead string so the repeating structure is visible.
State the rule in your own words: 'each time we add 5'. Predict the NEXT term before extending.
Predict the ones digit of the next three terms (25, 30, 35) and say why ('they alternate 5, 0, 5').

TEST it: have the adult reveal the next term of the given sequence (e.g. uncover a hidden card or the next group on the bead string) and compare it with your prediction; if it does not match, revise the rule. Extending the sequence yourself with your own rule is not a test.
Then say how you could be sure a rule is right before trusting it.
activities.insight: A rule guessed from a couple of cases should be tested on fresh cases before we rely on it: a passing test makes us more confident (it does not prove the rule), while one failing case shows the rule needs revising — this is the MP8 discipline of checking a generalisation.

activities.title: Subtracting 10 on a hundred square — and bounding the rule
steps: On a hundred square (or with place-value cards), start at a two-digit number such as 45 and subtract 10; land on 35 and notice the tens digit dropped by one while the ones digit stayed the same.
Repeat from two or three other starting numbers to see the same pattern each time; state the rule: 'take away 10 drops the tens digit by one'.
Test the boundary: does taking away ONE do the same thing? Try 45−1 (which gives 44) and see it does not — so the rule is only for −10.
Say the rule in your own words AND what it does NOT cover.
activities.insight: Subtracting 10 from a two-digit number lowers the tens digit by one and leaves the ones digit unchanged — and a good rule is stated with the conditions under which it holds.

activities.title: Check-in: which fact did you use?
steps: Answer short derivation prompts such as '6+6=12, so 6+7=__' and 'continue the sequence 5, 10, 15, __'.
For each answer, say WHICH known fact or rule you used to get it, not just the number.
Try at least one where you explain how you'd check your answer is reasonable.
activities.insight: Getting the right number is not enough; the target is reusing a known fact or rule and being able to justify it.

checkQuestion: You know 6 + 6 = 12. Use that to work out 6 + 7 quickly, without counting from one. Then tell me how it would help with 6 + 8.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child deriving from the known double: '6+7 is one more than 6+6, so 13; 6+8 is two more, so 14.' The reuse of the known fact and the adjustment, not just 13, is the target.
